name: Samuel Morris
title: Samuel Morris: a student from Liberia and a faith remembered
description: Samuel Kaboo Morris and his time at Taylor University from 1891: institutional facts, Christian memory and caution about extraordinary accounts.

sections.heading: A young man came seeking to learn
paragraphs: Samuel Morris, also known as Kaboo, came from Liberia to the United States in 1891. Taylor University preserves the memory of his desire to learn more about the Christian faith. The university dates his arrival at the Fort Wayne campus to December of that year, after he had been welcomed by Stephen Merritt in New York.

His presence left a deep impression on those who knew him. The institutional history recalls his prayer and his involvement in nearby churches. Morris died in May 1893. His time as a student was short, but his memory became linked to the identity and missionary calling of the institution.

sections.heading: A memory that should keep its sources
paragraphs: Taylor’s chronology identifies the biography published by its president Thaddeus Reade in 1896 as an important means of spreading Morris’s story. That information helps us understand how a personal memory became part of an institutional tradition, passed on through books, tributes and educational programs.

Taylor’s overview includes an extraordinary escape from captivity told by Morris. Here it is identified as testimony preserved by the university, not as an event confirmed by independent documentation. This distinction allows us to read religious memory with respect while staying clear about the kind of evidence available.

reflection: In 1 Timothy 4:12, Paul calls a young believer to set an example in conduct, love, faith and purity. That passage offers a way to reflect on Morris’s influence without depending on extraordinary details. A young life can carry weight in a community through a willingness to learn and the way it treats others.

The story also invites us to recognize African Christians as central figures in the church’s memory. Morris was a student seeking an education, and he left a mark on those who welcomed him. Telling his life with clear sources lets us appreciate that mark without reducing him to an exotic figure or presenting every later tradition as proven fact.
review_note: Both sources are institutional, not independent corroboration. The birth date is approximate, and supernatural accounts are treated as testimony, not as externally verified facts.
